desc:
The array nums is a mountain: strictly increasing up to a peak (neither the first nor the last element), then strictly decreasing.

Return the smallest index i such that nums[i] == target, or -1 if the target does not occur. Because the same value can appear once on each slope, take care to prefer the left one. Use O(log n) time.

For example, in [1, 3, 5, 4, 3, 1] the target 3 occurs at indices 1 and 4, so the answer is 1.
constraints: nums is guaranteed to be a mountain array
hints: A normal binary search needs a sorted array, and a mountain is not sorted. But it consists of two sorted pieces.
Step 1: find the peak with a binary search on the slope (nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1]). Step 2: binary search the ascending part. Step 3: only if not found there, binary search the descending part.
Searching the left part first guarantees the smallest index. In the descending part flip the comparison: if nums[mid] > target go right, if it is smaller go left.
editorial: The peak splits the mountain into nums[0..peak], strictly ascending, and nums[peak + 1..n - 1], strictly descending. Both are sorted, so they can be searched independently by ordinary binary search (with the comparison reversed on the descending side).

Procedure: (1) find the peak in O(log n) by comparing nums[mid] with nums[mid + 1]; (2) binary search for target in [0, peak] and return the index if found; (3) otherwise binary search in [peak + 1, n - 1] using the descending order. Since every index of the left part is smaller than every index of the right part, answering from the left part first returns the smallest index.

Three logarithmic searches give O(log n) time and O(1) space. A common mistake is to return the first hit found anywhere without checking the left slope first, which breaks when the target occurs on both slopes.
